name: Catalog of Broken Promises
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Receipts: A Running List of Predictions That Did Not Land
lesson.summary: Moving from the general pattern to specifics, this chapter assembles a concrete list of named quantum computing predictions that failed to materialize on their stated timelines, forming the evidence base the rest of this unit draws on.
lesson.body:
The previous chapters established that quantum computing has a structural pattern of restating a three-to-five-year horizon roughly every five to ten years since Feynman's 1981 proposal, without that horizon ever visibly closing. A pattern is more convincing when it is anchored to specific, checkable examples rather than left as an abstract observation, so this chapter functions as a working catalog, a set of concrete claims made publicly, on the record, that can be checked against what actually happened by their stated deadline.

Cryptography is one of the clearest categories. Following Shor's 1994 algorithm, predictions circulated through the 1990s and 2000s that quantum computers capable of breaking widely used RSA encryption were roughly a decade away, a claim repeated at intervals through the 2000s and 2010s. As of the mid-2020s, no publicly known quantum computer has broken real-world RSA encryption at deployed key lengths, and the cryptography community's own consensus timelines for cryptographically relevant quantum computers have themselves been repeatedly pushed later with each passing decade, even as organizations began migrating to post-quantum cryptographic standards as a precaution.

Commercial quantum advantage is another category, covered in the zero-ROI chapter: specific claims that quantum computers would outperform classical machines on real business optimization or simulation problems within a few years of Google's 2019 Sycamore result did not materialize by 2025 in any publicly verified, independently reproduced case. D-Wave's own history, covered next, supplies a further specific example, where a 2007 commercial launch was followed by years of independent studies unable to confirm the promised quantum speedup on real problems. IBM's own roadmap revisions, covered later in this unit, provide a fourth category, where the company's stated near-term milestones for error-corrected, fault-tolerant systems were revised and pushed later multiple times between the 2020 roadmap and the 2023 Condor-era updates.

It is worth being precise about what this catalog does and does not show. It does not show that the underlying physics is wrong, that the researchers involved were acting in bad faith, or that no progress has occurred; hardware metrics have genuinely improved across every one of these examples. What it shows is that the specific, dated, public-facing predictions attached to each milestone have a consistent track record of arriving late relative to their own stated timeline, often by years, and sometimes by more than a decade. That track record is the appropriate baseline against which to weigh any new prediction made about quantum computing's near future.

This catalog is deliberately not exhaustive, and it will keep growing as more specific claims come due. Readers evaluating a new quantum computing announcement can use it as a template: identify the specific, checkable prediction buried inside the announcement, note the stated deadline, and revisit it when that deadline arrives, exactly the process that produced every entry already on this list. The next several chapters apply this same method to particular companies and institutions, starting with D-Wave, whose 2007 commercial launch is one of the earliest and most thoroughly documented entries in the catalog.
